title: Caramel Colour Rules and Practice | Craft Beer School
desc: Where caramel colouring is allowed in whisky, what E150a is and how a distillery doses it for batch consistency without changing flavour.
teaser: Caramel is not there to fool anyone. Used properly, it keeps batch two the same colour as batch one.
standfirst: Caramel colour is one of the few things that may be added to some whiskies besides water. The rules depend on the category and the country. The practice, when it is done well, is about consistency in tiny amounts.
sections:
The caramel used in whisky is spirit caramel, coded E150a, also called plain caramel. It is made by heating sugars under controlled conditions until they turn a deep brown. It is used in very small amounts to adjust colour. At those amounts it should add no noticeable flavour.

Other caramel classes exist, made with additions such as sulphites or ammonia compounds, but they are not the ones whisky rules permit. Our guide to tannin and colour from the cask explains where whisky's natural colour comes from.
Where it is allowed and where it is not

The rules differ by category:

  • Scotch whisky. Plain caramel colouring (E150a) is the only permitted addition besides water.
  • Irish whiskey. Plain caramel is also permitted. Our guide to the rules that define Irish whiskey covers the rest.
  • Bourbon. No colouring is allowed. Its colour comes from new charred oak alone.

Labelling also varies. Some markets, Germany being the well known example, require a declaration that colouring has been added. In India, the FSSAI standards for alcoholic beverages and state rules set what may be added and declared. These change, so check the current notification for every market you sell into.

Casks vary. Two batches of the same whisky, built from different casks, can come out noticeably different in colour while tasting much the same. Retailers and drinkers notice the colour difference first and may assume the whisky has changed. A small caramel adjustment brings each batch to the same target colour.

That is the honest use. The dishonest use is darkening a young whisky to suggest age or sherry cask influence. Many enthusiasts dislike caramel for this reason. A growing number of producers state no added colour on the label.

Caramel is concentrated, so work with a dilution. A practical method:

  1. Make a stock solution of caramel in reduced whisky or demineralised water, say 1 part caramel to 99 parts liquid, by weight.
  2. Set a colour reference: a retained sample of the target batch or a measured value from a colorimeter.
  3. Add the stock to sample bottles of the new batch in measured steps and compare each against the reference in the same light.
  4. Scale up the dose that matches, in proportion to the batch volume.
  5. Mix thoroughly in the tank and check colour again before bottling.

The floor detail we insist on: dissolve the caramel in a small volume of liquid first and add that, never neat syrup into a big tank. Thick caramel sinks, sticks to the tank bottom and leaves the first bottles darker than the last.

At typical doses, caramel affects only colour. Push the dose high and it can add a faint bitter or burnt sugar note. If you need a lot of caramel to reach the target, the problem is the casks, not the colour. Rebalance the cask mix instead.

Measure colour with an instrument where you can. A simple colorimeter or a comparator reading gives a number to put in the batch record. Human eyes judge colour differently under warm and cool light. A shop under bright LEDs changes it again.
Decide your policy before your first release

The first decision is whether you use caramel at all. Some craft distilleries skip it as part of their identity and accept batch variation. Others use it carefully and say so. Both positions are defensible. Changing your mind after launch is harder, because label claims and customer expectations follow the first release.

Write the policy into your product specification: permitted or not, target colour value, maximum dose and the measurement method. Our guide to chill filtration and caramel colouring covers how drinkers see these choices.
Consistency is a system, not a fix

Caramel solves a symptom. The underlying task is managing cask variation so batches stay close in colour and flavour. Cask selection, blend records and colour measurement together do most of the work. Caramel trims the last small difference. Learning to build that system is something a distilling course covers far better than a bottle of syrup can.

Your first step: measure the colour of your last three batches with the same method in the same light and write the numbers side by side.
faqs: E150a is plain caramel, also called spirit caramel. It is made by heating sugars and is the only caramel class permitted in Scotch whisky.
Is caramel colour allowed in bourbon?
No. Bourbon may not contain added colouring. Its colour comes from maturation in new charred oak containers.
Does caramel colour change the taste of whisky?
At the small doses used for colour correction it should not be noticeable. High doses can add a faint bitter or burnt sugar note.
Do whisky labels have to declare caramel?
It depends on the market. Some countries, such as Germany, require a declaration. Check the current rules for each market, including FSSAI and state rules in India.
